story.intro:
**Welcome to StatsQuest.** This is a short game about statistics for modeling and simulation.

**Your mission:** help a simulation team make decisions from data. You will practice center, spread, distributions, arrivals, and Monte Carlo simulation.

Start with a quick confidence check-in. Then play each level, earn XP, and unlock the next step. The final check-out shows what changed. Check-ins do not affect XP.
story.pre_assessment: Rate your confidence on five topics. This is not a quiz. It gives you a starting point to compare with the end.
story.post_assessment: Answer five check-out questions, then rate your confidence again on the same five topics from the start. That's what shows how much changed for you.

levels.1: Outliers can change the mean. Compare mean, median, and mode.
levels.2: Two datasets can have the same mean but different spread.
levels.3: Match each situation to the right distribution.
levels.4: Use Poisson for counts and Exponential for wait times.
levels.5: Run many simulations to see possible outcomes.

story.epilogue: Finished. You completed the statistics path and the final simulation challenge.

home.title: Introduction and overview
home.description: Why statistics helps us model real systems, like airport lines and product defects.

level_1.title: Mean, median, and mode
level_1.description: Shows how to find the center of data and why median can help with outliers.

level_2.title: Range, variance, and standard deviation
level_2.description: Explains range, variance, standard deviation, and why spread matters.

level_3.title: From data to distributions and Normal distribution
level_3.description: Shows how data shapes become distributions, including the Normal curve.

level_3.title: Uniform distribution
level_3.description: Covers situations where every value in a range is equally likely.

level_3.title: Bernoulli and Binomial distributions
level_3.description: Connects one yes/no trial to counting successes across many trials.

level_3.title: Poisson distribution
level_3.description: Models event counts in a fixed time, like arrivals per 10 minutes.

level_4.title: Simulation realism
level_4.description: Shows why random inputs make simulations more realistic.

level_5.title: Monte Carlo idea
level_5.description: Shows why we run simulations many times.

formulas.home:
Formula quick reference

**Mean:** add all values, then divide by how many values there are.  
Formula: $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}$

**Median:** sort the values, then take the middle value.

**Mode:** find the value that appears most often.

**Range:** subtract the smallest value from the largest value.  
Formula: $\text{Range} = \max - \min$

**Variance:** measures spread using squared distances from the mean.  
Formula: $s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}$

**Standard deviation:** take the square root of variance.  
Formula: $s = \sqrt{s^2}$

hints.L3_Q1: Does the value cluster around a center, or is it spread evenly across a range?
hints.L3_Q2: This describes exactly one trial with two possible outcomes.
hints.L3_Q3: You're counting successes across a fixed number of separate yes/no trials.
hints.L3_Q4: No value in the range is any more likely than another.
hints.L3_BONUS: This is about the waiting time until the next event, not a count.
hints.L4_POISSON: You are counting how many passengers arrive during a fixed 10-minute block.
hints.L4_EXP: You are measuring the gap in time before one single passenger shows up next.

scaffold_fading.level_1: Guided practice: predict, experiment, observe, explain, transfer.
scaffold_fading.level_2: Guided practice with less help: inspect the data before seeing the spread statistics.
scaffold_fading.level_3: Challenge first: use hints only when needed.
scaffold_fading.level_4: Independent lab: ask for help only if needed.

level_copy.home_mission: Complete five levels: center, spread, distributions, arrivals, and Monte Carlo simulation.
level_copy.level_1_intro: A team is studying student commute times. Start with the usual pattern, make a prediction, then test what happens when one commute becomes unusually long.
level_copy.level_1_prediction: Prediction: What do you think will happen if we replace 35 with 600?
level_copy.level_1_observe: Did the result match your prediction?
level_copy.level_1_outlier_input: Enter a **very large outlier** to replace the final commute time
level_copy.level_1_outlier_caption: Try values like 90, 200, or 600 and watch the statistics change.
level_copy.level_1_q1: Which **measure of center** changes the most because of the **very large outlier**?
level_copy.level_1_q1_explanation: The mean uses every value, so one very large value pulls it up.
level_copy.level_1_transition: Now transfer the idea to a new setting.
level_copy.level_1_hospital_intro: A hospital usually sees wait times close to 10 minutes.
level_copy.level_1_hospital_prompt: One patient waited much longer than usual. The hospital wants one number to describe a typical patient's wait.
level_copy.level_1_q2: Which statistic would you report for the **typical wait**?
level_copy.level_1_q2_explanation: The median stays close to the usual waits because one unusually long wait does not pull it much.
level_copy.level_1_reflection: Complete the sentence: When data contains an extreme outlier, I should check ______ before describing a typical value.
level_copy.level_1_bonus_q: If one value becomes a **very large outlier** and the smallest value stays the same, what happens to the **range**?
level_copy.level_1_bonus_explanation: Range is maximum minus minimum. If the maximum gets larger and the minimum stays the same, the range increases.
level_copy.level_2_focus: Level 2 is about **spread**: how close together or far apart the values are.
level_copy.level_2_intro: Two machines make parts near 10 units. Look at the values first, then decide which machine is more consistent.
level_copy.level_2_q1: Both machines have the same **mean**. Which machine is more **consistent**?
level_copy.level_2_q1_explanation: Machine A's values stay closer to 10, so its standard deviation is smaller.
level_copy.level_2_prediction: Prediction before the slider: What do you think increasing standard deviation from 5 to 20 will do?
level_copy.level_2_sd_input: Choose a standard deviation for a process
level_copy.level_2_sd_caption: A larger standard deviation means values are farther from the mean.
level_copy.level_2_chart_caption: A larger standard deviation makes the chart wider.
level_copy.level_2_q2: As **standard deviation** increases, what happens to the **data values** in the chart?
level_copy.level_2_q2_explanation: Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.
level_copy.level_2_bonus_q: Which quantity is the square of the **standard deviation**?
level_copy.level_4_prediction: Prediction: If the average arrival rate doubles, what do you think happens to the average wait between passengers?
level_copy.level_4_observe: Did the result match your prediction?
level_copy.level_5_prediction: Prediction: As the number of simulation runs grows from 10 to 10,000, what do you think happens to the histogram of possible workloads?
level_copy.level_5_observe: Did the result match your prediction? Try changing the runs above to compare.
